I work on heart drugs, so please be patient with me. Why exactly does leprosy cause pain?
It is a fair question. The bacteria live inside the nerve, so the body attacks the nerve itself.
The body attacks its own nerve? Because of the bacteria?
Exactly. The attack causes inflammation, and the inflammation leads to damage. Since the nerve is damaged, it sends the wrong signals.
And that is the pain. But your poster says many patients also feel nothing. That seems like the opposite.
That's what makes it so interesting, because both come from the same damage. Some fibers stop working, and as a result the patient feels nothing. Others send pain all the time.
We see something similar with diabetes in my hospital. Is the pain related to how long the patient waited?
Very much. Late diagnosis is the biggest factor. Therefore, our message to clinics is simple: look at the feet early.
So a better outcome depends on an early look, not on a stronger drug. I did not expect that from a pharmacologist.
Neither did I, at the beginning. That is why I am here.

Let me explain the main result of our study, because it surprised our own team. We gave the same drug to two groups of patients with nerve pain. In the first group, the pain went down after six weeks. In the second group, almost nothing changed. So we asked why. The answer was not the drug. It was the time. The second group started treatment two years after the first symptoms, and because of that delay, the nerve damage was already permanent. Since the damage was older, the drug had less to protect. As a result, we now say one thing to every clinic: the first factor is not the dose, it is the date. Early treatment leads to a better outcome. Therefore, our next study is about diagnosis, not about new drugs.

Thank you for the question. Why did so many patients stop the treatment? There were three factors, and they are connected. First, many of our patients live far from the clinic. Because of the distance, one single visit costs them a full day of work. Second, the drug has side effects in the first two weeks, so some patients felt worse before they felt better. And third, nobody explained this to them at the start. Since they did not expect the side effects, they thought the drug was making them sick. As a result, almost one third stopped in the first month. Therefore, we changed only one thing: a ten-minute conversation before the first dose. The next year, only one patient in ten stopped.
